story.headline: US sanctions ICC president
story.summary: The US Treasury sanctioned ICC President Tomoko Akane of Japan and senior trial lawyer Abdoulaye Seye of Senegal, the sharpest escalation yet against the court.
story.display_body: The United States sanctioned the president of the International Criminal Court, Japan's Tomoko Akane, and a senior ICC trial lawyer, Senegal's Abdoulaye Seye, on Tuesday 18 August. the sharpest escalation yet in the Trump administration's campaign against The Hague-based court. The US Treasury added both to its sanctions list under the executive order Washington issued against the ICC earlier this year; Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the two had "directly engaged" in ICC efforts to investigate or prosecute officials of governments that have not accepted the court's jurisdiction — the wording points at the court's warrants touching US and Israeli officials, though the administration frames the whole institution as "politicized." Treasury issued a general licence allowing existing dealings with Akane to be wound down by 17 September. Japan's government called the move "very regrettable," a rare public rebuke of Washington from a close G7 ally over one of its own nationals.
story.why: Sanctioning the sitting head of the world's permanent war-crimes court — and a Japanese jurist at that — targets the institution itself rather than a case, and puts a G7 government in the position of protesting sanctions on its own citizen. The ICC's ability to function depends on banks, staff, and states not treating association with its leadership as a legal risk; that is precisely what the designation is designed to create.

story.headline: Israel bombs Syrian air base
story.summary: Israel struck the Abu Duhur air base in Idlib, Syria to stop Turkish troops deploying there, drawing condemnation from Syria and Turkey.
story.display_body: Israel struck the Abu Duhur air base in Syria's northwestern Idlib province early Tuesday 18 August, saying the aim was to stop Turkish forces from deploying there. Israeli state accounts and Syrian state TV described roughly eight strikes on the runway, causing damage but no reported casualties. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office said Syria had been "on the verge of breaching" an agreed security "status quo" by letting Turkish troops move in, and that Israel had warned Damascus the deployment would threaten its security. Syria's foreign minister, Asaad al-Shibani, condemned the raid as an "unjustified provocation" and a violation of sovereignty; Turkey's foreign ministry also condemned it, and Qatar, Egypt and Saudi Arabia issued statements against the strikes.
story.why: The strike opens a direct friction point between Israel and Turkey — two US-aligned militaries — over who gets to operate inside post-Assad Syria, and signals Israel intends to police a buffer around its northern frontier by force even against a NATO member's plans.

story.headline: France enacts assisted-dying law
story.summary: Macron promulgated France's assisted-dying law, making medical aid in dying legal for terminally ill adults after the Constitutional Council cleared it.
story.display_body: France's assisted-dying law was promulgated by President Emmanuel Macron and formally took effect on Wednesday 19 August, making medical aid in dying legal for the first time. The step follows the Constitutional Council's ruling on Friday 14 August that found no grounds to strike the text down, which itself followed the National Assembly's final adoption on 15 July after years of debate. Under the law, adults with a "serious and incurable" illness in an advanced or terminal phase, suffering that cannot be relieved, may request assistance to die; access will phase in as implementing decrees follow. It is one of France's most consequential social reforms in a decade.
story.why: France joins the small group of European states with a legal right to die, resolving a debate that has run through French politics for years — and the outcome next door feeds directly into how Switzerland, which already permits assisted suicide, and its neighbours frame their own end-of-life rules.

story.headline: France to expel two Iranian diplomats
story.summary: France announced it will expel two Iranian diplomats in retaliation for the July detention of two French diplomats in Tehran.
story.display_body: France announced on Tuesday 18 August that it will expel two Iranian diplomats. in retaliation for what Paris says was the "deliberate" assault and hours-long detention of two of its own diplomats in Tehran on 19 July. Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said the "intolerable act would have consequences"; Iran's foreign ministry responded that the two French diplomats would not be allowed to return to Iran. The July incident is entangled with the continued detention of two Iranian graphic-design artists arrested during a cultural meeting with the French officials.

story.headline: Federal Council seeks 970M for air defence
story.summary: The Swiss Federal Council asked parliament for a 970-million-franc supplementary credit to speed up ground-based air-defence procurement.
story.display_body: The Federal Council asked parliament on Wednesday 19 August for a supplementary credit of about 970 million francs to speed up the build-out of Switzerland's air defence, plus a further 100 million for civil protection. The request (a Nachtragskredit — an in-year addition to the approved budget) breaks down as roughly 250 million francs for shorter-range ground-based air defence, 650 million for medium-range systems, 60 million for radar and 10 million for defending against mini-drones. The government says the money is needed for advance payments to lock in delivery slots, arguing that surging global demand has stretched arms-makers' production and lengthened lead times, so manufacturers now want substantial money up front. It cites a "heightened threat situation" as the justification.
story.why: The credit is a concrete measure of how far Switzerland's post-neutrality-debate rearmament has moved from principle to cash — and it commits money before parliament has finished the larger fight over how to fund the army, including the temporary VAT rise the Council has separately proposed.

story.headline: Swiss individual taxation delayed to 2032
story.summary: The Federal Council set 2032 as the entry-into-force date for the switch to individual taxation.
story.display_body: The switch to individual taxation in Switzerland will not take effect until 2032, the Federal Council confirmed on Wednesday 19 August. years later than campaigners had hoped. The reform would tax spouses separately rather than jointly, ending the long-criticised "marriage penalty" under which some two-earner couples pay more than two unmarried earners on the same income; the delayed date reflects the scale of the changeover for cantonal tax authorities and IT systems. The reform still faces a likely referendum.
story.why: For two-income households in Switzerland this is the reform that decides whether marriage carries a tax cost — and a 2032 start means the current joint-taxation rules, and the penalty they can impose, stay in place for years yet.

story.headline: Cuprate superconducts in a single copper-oxygen plane
story.summary: A cuprate thinned to one CuO2 plane still superconducts, isolating the 2D limit of high-Tc physics.
story.display_body: Cuprates — copper-oxide ceramics that superconduct (carry current with zero resistance) at unusually high temperatures — are built from stacked CuO₂ (copper–oxygen) planes, and a long-standing question is how few of those planes the effect actually needs. Borrowing the top-down, sticky-tape exfoliation trick that made graphene, a Fudan-led team thinned a cuprate all the way down to a single CuO₂ plane and still measured superconductivity, isolating the truly two-dimensional limit of the problem. Earlier work had shown the essential physics fits within two planes; pushing to one strips the system to what may be its minimal ingredient.
story.why: If one copper–oxygen layer is enough to superconduct, theories of high-temperature superconductivity can be tested against the barest possible system — a cleaner route toward understanding, and someday designing, better superconductors.

story.headline: Graphene device measures one-third of an electron
story.summary: An EPFL antidot device reads the e/3 charge of fractional quantum Hall quasiparticles directly.
story.display_body: In the fractional quantum Hall effect — what emerges when electrons are confined to two dimensions in an intense magnetic field — the electron fluid gives rise to "quasiparticles" that act as if they carry only a fraction of an electron's charge. Measuring that fraction cleanly is hard, because the usual interferometer designs entangle bulk and edge contributions. The EPFL-led team instead built an antidot — a controllable bump in the device's potential landscape that behaves as a tunable artificial impurity — into a graphene sample and read the charge of quasiparticles tunnelling through it, directly extracting values such as e/3 (one-third of the elementary charge).
story.why: A clean way to weigh fractional charges is a prerequisite for probing these quasiparticles' exotic quantum statistics — the same physics being courted for topological quantum computing. The lead group is Swiss.

story.headline: Chemists walk nitrogen around a pyridine ring
story.summary: A sequence of nitrogen insertion and deletion transposes a pyridine's nitrogen, relocating substituents.
story.display_body: Pyridines — six-membered aromatic rings carrying a single nitrogen, ubiquitous in drug molecules — behave very differently depending on where a substituent sits relative to that nitrogen, and normally each "positional isomer" (same atoms, different arrangement) must be built from scratch. The IBS/KAIST team report a way to reorganise the ring itself: a controlled sequence of nitrogen insertion and deletion transposes the nitrogen to a new position, relocating the attached groups without changing their identity. A companion paper from Cambridge performs related "skeletal editing" on tertiary benzylamines, rewriting their core carbon–nitrogen connectivity late in a synthesis (Nature, University of Cambridge).
story.why: Skeletal editing lets chemists remodel a molecule's core in the final steps instead of redesigning a whole synthesis — a faster lane for exploring drug-like variants around a promising scaffold.

story.headline: Blood test flags immunotherapy benefit in lung cancer
story.summary: Circulating-tumour-DNA clearance tracks who gains from perioperative nivolumab in resectable NSCLC.
story.display_body: In resectable non-small-cell lung cancer (a lung tumour still removable by surgery), the CheckMate 77T trial had already shown that giving the immunotherapy nivolumab before and after surgery improves event-free survival; this analysis asks who benefits. Following circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA — fragments of tumour genome shed into the blood) in the biomarker-evaluable patients (41% of those randomised), the team found ctDNA detectable in 85% before treatment and 92% by the end of pre-surgery dosing, and that clearing it during that window tracked with benefit.
story.why: A blood test that signals whether immunotherapy is working before the operation could help spare non-responders unnecessary treatment and flag who needs more — though this is a retrospective subgroup analysis, not yet a decision rule.

story.headline: In-vivo CRISPR screen reads T cells inside tumours
story.summary: A mouse model recovers human T cells from solid tumours, enabling genome-wide in-vivo CRISPR screens.
story.display_body: Finding genetic tweaks that help immune cells attack solid tumours is a central goal of cell therapy, but the genes that matter inside a living tumour often stay hidden in lab-dish (in-vitro) screens. The UCSF/Gladstone team built a mouse model that efficiently recovers human T cells from solid tumours, making genome-wide CRISPR screens — systematically switching off each gene to see which alter T-cell behaviour — feasible with only a handful of animals. The tumour-infiltrating cells showed the classic signs of "exhaustion," the dysfunctional state that blunts immunotherapy, giving the screen a realistic setting to map its drivers.
story.why: A screen that mirrors the hostile tumour environment can surface engineering targets that dish experiments miss — grist for the next generation of CAR-T and tumour-infiltrating-lymphocyte therapies.

story.headline: Distant galaxies hide mass in dim dwarf stars
story.summary: JWST spectra of z~0.7 galaxies show a bottom-heavy stellar mix, implying extra hidden stellar mass.
story.display_body: A galaxy's stellar mass is inferred from its light, but that conversion hinges on the initial mass function (IMF) — the assumed spread of star masses at birth, usually copied from the Milky Way. Faint low-mass stars dominate the mass yet contribute little light, so the low-mass end is normally guessed, not measured. Using ultra-deep JWST spectra of nine massive quiescent galaxies at redshift z ≈ 0.7 (light that left them roughly 6 billion years ago), the Leiden-led team constrained that low-mass end directly and found the IMF "bottom-heavy" — richer in dwarf stars than the Milky Way's, implying more hidden stellar mass than standard assumptions give.
story.why: JWST has turned up early galaxies that look almost too massive to exist so soon; a bottom-heavy IMF shows galaxies really can carry extra unseen stellar mass, which bears on how the masses — and the assembly speed — of the earliest galaxies are read. The measurement is at intermediate redshift, so it informs rather than settles the high-redshift debate.

story.headline: First globular-cluster stream found beyond Milky Way
story.summary: A tidal stream from a globular cluster is found around an ultra-diffuse galaxy, a new dark-matter probe.
story.display_body: Stellar streams — thin ribbons of stars pulled from a cluster by a galaxy's tides — trace the host's gravity, and so its dark matter. Until now, globular-cluster streams were known only in the Milky Way. In deep Hubble Space Telescope imaging of the ultra-diffuse galaxy UGC 9050-Dw1 (a galaxy as sprawling as the Milky Way but with very few stars), a Copenhagen-led team found evidence for the first such stream around another galaxy, and used generative modelling of its shape to weigh the progenitor cluster.
story.why: Extragalactic streams open a new way to map dark matter well beyond the Milky Way — including the puzzling ultra-diffuse galaxies whose dark-matter content is fiercely debated.

story.headline: Deimos shaped by one glancing impact
story.summary: Simulations tie Deimos's smooth surface and south-polar basin to a single subcatastrophic impact.
story.display_body: Deimos, the smaller, 12-km Martian moon, is oddly smooth and coated in fine regolith (loose surface dust), unlike its heavily cratered sibling Phobos, and its shape is dominated by one large south-polar depression. Simulations by the Bern-led team show a single oblique impact from a roughly 320-metre projectile can quantitatively reproduce that depression, the global dust blanket, and finer features such as bright streaks and infilled craters — a "subcatastrophic" hit that remodelled the moon without breaking it apart.
story.why: Tying Deimos's odd surface to a single impact sharpens the science targets for JAXA's planned Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission to the two moons. The lead group is Swiss.

story.headline: Milky Way's oldest known merger revealed
story.summary: Dated globular clusters point to a major Milky Way merger 1.8 Gyr before Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus.
story.display_body: The Milky Way grew by devouring smaller galaxies, and the largest early merger securely known — Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus (a dwarf galaxy that fell in) — dates to about 10 billion years ago. Using globular clusters as tracers and a new method to date them, the INAF Bologna-led team found the clusters split into three distinct age–metallicity sequences: one native to the proto-Milky Way, one from Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus, and one pointing to an earlier, previously unrecognised major accretion event some 1.8 billion years before it.
story.why: Each identified merger is a chapter in the Galaxy's origin story; finding an even older one pushes back the clock on when the Milky Way began assembling in earnest.
